subject: Accounting
title: Wirecard: Germany's Enron
description: Learn Wirecard: Germany's Enron in one minute.

hook.text: Wirecard claimed to have €1.9 billion in cash. The bank said the accounts didn't exist.

buildup.text: The German fintech company processed payments for merchants worldwide and joined the DAX index.

discovery.text: For years, reporters at the Financial Times flagged irregularities. Wirecard sued the journalists.

twist.text: Germany's financial regulator investigated the journalists instead of Wirecard.

climax.text: When auditors demanded proof of cash, it didn't exist. Wirecard collapsed in days.

punchline.text: €1.9 billion in cash. Zero in reality.

quiz.question: What did auditors discover about Wirecard's reported cash?
options: The cash was in a different currency
It was invested in real estate

details.summary: Wirecard, once a jewel of Germany's tech sector worth €24 billion, collapsed in 2020 when €1.9 billion in supposed bank balances turned out not to exist. This topic covers the longest-running fraud in modern European history and the stunning regulatory failure that allowed it.
details.whyItMatters: Wirecard exposed catastrophic failures in German financial regulation, where the regulator actually attacked the journalists trying to expose the fraud instead of investigating the company.
takeaways: Wirecard claimed €1.9 billion in bank accounts held in the Philippines that didn't exist
Germany's regulator BaFin targeted journalists and short sellers instead of investigating Wirecard itself
CEO Markus Braun was arrested; COO Jan Marsalek is a fugitive believed to be in Russia

faq.question: What was the Wirecard scandal?
faq.answer: Wirecard, a German payment processing company valued at €24 billion, fabricated €1.9 billion in bank balances and inflated revenue through fictitious transactions in Asia. When auditors finally confirmed the money didn't exist in June 2020, the company collapsed within days.

faq.question: Why did regulators fail to catch the Wirecard fraud?
faq.answer: Germany's BaFin regulator treated Wirecard as a technology company rather than a financial institution, limiting its oversight. Worse, when the Financial Times published evidence of fraud, BaFin filed criminal complaints against the journalists and banned short-selling of Wirecard stock.
